passage:
Yusuf had forty rupees in his tin, and the shop window held a remote-control car that cost four hundred. Every Sunday he stood in front of it. His friends bought sweets and sticker packets. Yusuf's fingers twitched near a pack of cricket cards.
"Buy it, beta, it's your money," said his mother Binita.
"I'll wait," said Yusuf.
"Next month?"
"Maybe two."
At home he drew ten squares on a sheet of paper and coloured one in each time he added coins. Binita had told him the shopkeeper would keep the car aside for him, and every Sunday the shopkeeper nodded at the window.
Three months later Yusuf carried the box home, and it felt heavier and better than any sweet.

qa.q: How many rupees did Yusuf have in his tin at the start?
What is Yusuf feeling as he stands at the shop window and passes the cricket cards?
qa.a: He is tempted but determined. His fingers twitch near the cards, yet he says he will wait for the car.

qa.q: What choice helped Yusuf keep saving?
qa.a: He drew ten squares and coloured one each time he added coins, so his progress was visible, and he trusted that the shopkeeper would keep the car aside.

qa.q: How might Binita feel watching Yusuf choose to wait?
qa.a: Probably proud and a little amazed, since she says it is his money but he decides to wait.

grounding: A child saves pocket money for a bigger toy instead of spending it, trusting the reward will arrive.

passage:
Vaibhav: Tarun, look, the fair has jalebis! Aren't you buying one?
Tarun: No, Mama. I'm saving for the football.
Vaibhav: One jalebi won't hurt.
Tarun: Last time you said, "Wait till Diwali," and you did take me. So I believe you'll take me for the football too.
Vaibhav: I will. How much have you got?
Tarun: Eighty-five rupees. Two more months.
Vaibhav: That's a long time.
Tarun: It's okay. I look at the picture every night. And I keep the coins in a tin, so I can't cheat.
Vaibhav: Then I'll buy the jalebi and you hold it while I eat.
Tarun: Ha! Deal.

qa.q: How many rupees does Tarun have saved?
Why is Tarun able to say no to the jalebi, and what is Tarun feeling about the football?
qa.a: Tarun feels confident and hopeful because Vaibhav kept the earlier promise about Diwali, so Tarun trusts the football promise too.

qa.q: What habits help Tarun keep waiting?
qa.a: Tarun looks at the football picture every night and keeps the coins in a tin so they cannot be spent.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav be thinking when Tarun mentions the Diwali promise?
qa.a: Vaibhav may feel touched and a little responsible, since Tarun's patience depends on Vaibhav keeping the promise.

grounding: A child chooses to save for a bigger reward, trusting that promised rewards actually arrive.
